paragraph: Bharata`s grave face with a far away look in his eyes, did not seem to notice much, for a premonition of some great ill haunted him to distraction. Close to Ayodhya, at Ujjihanagar, Bharata ordered the fastest horses to be harnessed to his chariot and sped towards Ayodhya, like the god of the winds, passing through space. Even the horses seemed to feel the restless urgency of their master.After traveling for seven days and seven nights they reached the outer bounds of Kosala and at dawn of the eighth day, Bharata beheld the golden turrets of Ayodhya, magnificent capital of the Ikshvakus built by lord Manu.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Bharata is deeply troubled by an intense premonition of impending disaster, causing him significant distress and distracting him from his surroundings. This overwhelming sense of foreboding drives him to rush towards Ayodhya with extreme urgency, even his horses seemingly mirroring his frantic pace.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage emphasizes the profound impact of intuition and premonition on an individual's state of mind and actions. Bharata's grave demeanor and distracted state highlight the psychological burden of a strong sense of impending doom. His urgent journey reflects his desperate attempt to confront or understand the source of his inner turmoil, prioritizing this internal unease above all else.
Outcome/Resolution: Driven by a persistent and distressing premonition, Bharata travels with extraordinary speed for seven days and nights. On the eighth day, he finally reaches Ayodhya, still under the heavy influence of his foreboding feelings.
Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Bharata is consumed by an 'Ashubha Nimitta' (inauspicious premonition) of a great ill, leading to deep 'Chinta' (anxiety) and 'Duhkha' (distress). This spiritual foreboding compels him to hasten his journey to Ayodhya, suggesting a subconscious pull towards destiny or a cosmic unfolding of events he instinctively senses.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Bharata experiences intense anticipatory anxiety and a pervasive sense of dread, manifesting as a 'premonition of some great ill' that 'haunted him to distraction.' His urgency and the horses' mirrored 'restless urgency' reflect a psychological drive to resolve this unsettling internal state, even before external events confirm his fears. His grave and distant demeanor are classic signs of preoccupation with internal distress.
